title: Watchfulness
hook: the first rung: simply paying attention to how you live

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Mesillat Yesharim, and your line: the path of the just. Today, the bottom rung of Luzzatto's ladder.

Some evenings the drive home simply disappears. Keys in the door, coat on the hook, and no memory of a single traffic light. The body made every turn. Nobody was watching. Plenty of days go that way too: answered, eaten, scrolled, slept, with the person living them somewhere else. Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto put a remedy for that on the very bottom rung of his ladder. Before zeal, before purity, before holiness, the first trait he asks for is the one that makes the others possible.
screen: `THE DRIVE HOME DISAPPEARS.` → `NOBODY WAS WATCHING.` → `THE BOTTOM RUNG.`

segments.voice: Zehirut. Watchfulness. Turn it four ways. First, what it is. In Mesillat Yesharim, watchfulness means a person looks carefully at their own deeds and ways: is this good, is this not, where is it heading? Not a mood. A habit of checking. Second, life without it. Someone who goes through life without watching, Luzzatto says, is like a blind man walking along the bank of a river. The danger is real and close, and he doesn't see it. Nothing has gone wrong yet, and that's what makes the riverbank frightening. Third, why people skip it. Luzzatto doesn't blame laziness first. He blames the rush: daily life presses so hard that people never get a quiet moment to look where they're going. He reaches for a line from Jeremiah about a horse charging headlong into battle, too fast to see what's in front of it. A good-hearted person can still be that horse. Fourth, the Tanakh's short version. The prophet Haggai, speaking to people busy with their own houses while the Temple lay unbuilt, says it twice: "Consider your ways." Some Mussar teachers pair this with heshbon hanefesh, an accounting of the soul at day's end, but zehirut starts earlier: mid-day, mid-drive, catching yourself while it's happening. It isn't suspicion of yourself. It's being present for your own life, so the rest of the ladder has someone standing on it.
screen: `LOOK AT YOUR OWN DEEDS AND WAYS.` · `A BLIND MAN ON A RIVERBANK.` · `A HORSE RUSHING INTO BATTLE.` · `CONSIDER YOUR WAYS.` · then, large: `BE WATCHFUL.`

segments.voice: Choose one hour later today, the commute, an afternoon at your desk, the evening at home, and one thing to watch for in it: how you speak when tired, what your hands reach for when bored, whether you're really listening. Rehearse the moment of noticing, a small inner glance, a quiet there I am, with no judging and no fixing. Then simply notice yourself breathing right now, and if you pray, you can ask for open eyes.
Zehirut. Watchfulness: paying careful attention to how you live. The first rung of Luzzatto's ladder in Mesillat Yesharim. Today's word.
Your line: be watchful. Seeing yourself comes before fixing anything. Eyes open; see you soon.

howItsDone: Mussar students begin Mesillat Yesharim with zehirut, watchfulness, often practicing it by pausing during the day to notice their own actions, alongside a nightly accounting of the soul.

Holiness first; once you feel holy, the smaller traits follow by themselves.

Zehirut.meaning: Hebrew: watchfulness, careful attention to your deeds

Mesillat Yesharim.meaning: The Path of the Just, Luzzatto's book on character

Haggai.meaning: a Hebrew prophet who urged rebuilding the Temple

heshbon hanefesh.meaning: an accounting of the soul, often at day's end

Tanakh.meaning: the Hebrew Bible: Torah, Prophets and Writings

notes: Mesillat Yesharim ch. 2 paraphrased: watchfulness defined as examining one's deeds and ways; the blind man on the riverbank image; the pressure of daily busyness; the citation of Jeremiah 8:6 (horse rushing into battle). Confirm these are in chapter 2 (some may be in chapter 3) and fairly paraphrased.

Haggai 1:5 and 1:7 both contain 'Consider your ways' in JPS 1917 ('Now therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts: Consider your ways'); 'says it twice' is based on those two verses. Confirm. The lesson does not claim Luzzatto cites Haggai.
Heshbon hanefesh is mentioned as a pairing Mussar teachers 'often' make; it was the subject of day 1254. Confirm 'often' is acceptable.
Practice: the outline asks to watch yourself for an hour; with a two-minute sit, the sit is used to choose and rehearse the hour.

Editor: Haggai's audience was misdescribed as 'people rebuilding their lives'; now 'busy with their own houses while the Temple lay unbuilt' (Haggai 1:4, 1:9), which also fits Luzzatto's point about busyness. 'Mussar teachers often pair' softened to 'some'; smoothed one practice line.
